```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, eval = requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE))
```

{gratia} provides methods for checking a fitted model with {bayesplot} and comparing
its predictive performance with {loo}. The bayesplot methods compare observed
responses with responses simulated from the model. The loo methods approximate
how well the model predicts each observation when it is left out of fitting.
You can also use gratia's `log_lik()`, `appraise()` and
`posterior_predictive_plot()` without either optional package.

Some bayesplot plots, including `error_binned` and the leave-one-out PIT plots,
also require {rstantools}. Use `install.packages("rstantools")` to install it.

We simulate 100 independent Poisson counts with a curved relationship between
`x` and the log expected count:

```{r models-data}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
set.seed(278)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(100, -1, 1))
dat$y <- rpois(nrow(dat), exp(.3 + sin(3 * dat$x)))
```

We fit a Poisson model with a linear effect of `x` and another with a smooth
effect. Comparing them will show whether the extra flexibility improves
prediction.

```{r models}
linear <- gam(y ~ x, data = dat, family = poisson(), method = "REML")
smooth <- gam(y ~ s(x, k = 7), data = dat, family = poisson(), method = "REML")
```

## Compare observed responses with simulated datasets

For each coefficient draw, a posterior predictive check generates another
response at every fitting observation. The variation between these replicated
datasets includes coefficient uncertainty and response variation. We first
compare response distributions, then compare their standard deviations:

```{r predictive-checks}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "dens_overlay", n_draws = 20, seed = 42)
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "stat", stat = "sd", n_draws = 500, seed = 42)
```

The density overlay compares the overall distribution of counts. The second
plot shows whether the observed standard deviation is typical of the replicated
datasets. You can supply a function to `stat`, such as
`function(y) mean(y == 0)` to compare the proportion of zero counts. To display
simulated responses alone, use `prefix = "ppd"`.

Pooling observations can hide a discrepancy confined to part of the covariate
range. We compare mean counts separately for negative and positive `x`.
The grouping vector must follow the order of the observations used to fit the
model; a grouping variable from the model data can instead be supplied by name.

```{r grouped-check}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", n_draws = 500,
  group = factor(dat$x > 0, labels = c("negative x", "positive x")), seed = 42)
```

Rows excluded from the fit because of missing values are also excluded from
these checks. For binomial models, plots from bayesplot use success counts,
and the posterior predictive plots in gratia use proportions.
Use `response` to select a response
from a multivariate model (for example, `"response1"`) or a family component
from a grouped-family model (for example, `"component2"`).
For `gamm()` and `gamm4()` fits, `conditioning` chooses whether checks use
fitted group effects, new group effects or the extracted GAM component. See
the [model diagnostics article](model-checking.html) for these comparisons.

## Calculate log likelihoods at coefficient draws

`log_lik()` evaluates how likely each observed response is at each coefficient
draw. It returns log densities for continuous responses and log probabilities
for discrete responses. Rows are posterior draws and columns are the
observations used to fit the model. For observation `i` and draw `s` in the
unweighted Poisson example, the entry is
`dpois(y[i], lambda = mu[s, i], log = TRUE)`.

```{r log-likelihood}
ll <- gratia::log_lik(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
dim(ll)
head(attr(ll, "observation"))
attr(ll, "gratia")
```

These values include the likelihood's normalising constants and any fitting
weights. Smoothing penalties affect the coefficient draws and are excluded
from the likelihood calculation. A multivariate normal observation contributes
one joint log density for its response vector. In a grouped-family fit, each
observation contributes a value from its own family.

## Compare predictive performance with loo

Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) evaluates how well each observation is
predicted using the other observations. The loo package approximates these
predictions with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS), which reweights
the existing coefficient draws. In this example it approximates a refit
that holds the smoothing parameter fixed. `elpd_loo` estimates expected log
predictive density. Higher values indicate better estimated predictive
performance when models use the same observations and response scale. We
compare the linear and smooth models and inspect the quality of the
approximation for the smooth model.

```{r loo-comparison}
loo_linear <- loo::loo(linear, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
loo_smooth <- loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
loo::loo_compare(loo_linear, loo_smooth)
loo::pareto_k_table(loo_smooth)
```

`loo_compare()` ranks models by their estimated predictive performance. The
top model has `elpd_diff = 0`. Negative values indicate lower scores relative
to that model. `se_diff` is the standard error of the estimated difference.
Here the smooth model (`model2`, the second argument) ranks first. None of
its Pareto-k values exceed loo's threshold for reliable reweighting.

The methods return ordinary loo objects, so loo's plotting, model-comparison
and weighting tools are available. For an already extracted matrix of
independent Gaussian coefficient draws, the equivalent calculation is
`loo::loo(ll, r_eff = 1)`. `loo::waic(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)` also works.
Model methods evaluate likelihoods one observation at a time, avoiding a full
draws-by-observations matrix unless saved PSIS weights are requested.

Large Pareto-k values flag observations whose leave-one-out predictions are
hard to approximate by reweighting. Check for these values and for loo warnings
in both models before interpreting a difference. If reweighting is unreliable,
refit the model with the relevant observations left out or run a separate
cross-validation analysis. [loo's Pareto-k diagnostics](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html)

The leave-one-out probability integral transform (LOO-PIT) measures where each
observation falls in its own leave-one-out predictive distribution. The
response simulations and the likelihoods used to compute the PSIS weights
come from the same coefficient draws. If the predictive distributions are
well calibrated, the PIT values should be approximately uniform. The calculation
uses randomisation to handle ties for counts. The overlay compares the
distribution of the resulting PIT values with simulated uniform references.

```{r loo-plot, eval=requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("rstantools", quietly = TRUE)}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "loo_pit_overlay", n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
```

## Understand the posterior approximation

By default, gratia draws coefficients jointly from {mgcv}'s Gaussian approximation.
For a distributional GAM, this includes coefficients for each distribution
parameter. For multivariate-normal likelihoods, it also includes the fitted
precision-matrix coefficients. Scale, shape and other parameters outside the
coefficient vector stay at fitted values, as do smoothing parameters.

For Gaussian draws, `unconditional = TRUE` uses mgcv's corrected coefficient
covariance when available to approximately account for uncertainty in the
smoothing parameters. Pareto-k values assess the stability of the reweighting.
The accuracy of the Gaussian approximation to the coefficient posterior is a
separate question.

Pass coefficient-sampler arguments through `sampling_args`. The first calls
below request the corrected covariance; the last uses four Metropolis–Hastings
chains to draw coefficients:

```{r sampling-options, eval=FALSE}
# Extra sampler arguments are kept separate from loo and plotting arguments.
loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(unconditional = TRUE))
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, n_draws = 50, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(unconditional = TRUE))

# Four chains share the total retained count, with separate burn-in.
loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(method = "mh", chains = 4, burnin = 1000))
```

For supplied coefficient draws, use `method = "user", draws = B` in
`log_lik()`, or place those arguments in `sampling_args` for loo and bayesplot.
LOO uses the chain and iteration mapping stored by gratia's samplers. For an
unlabelled matrix, supply `chain_id` or an explicit `r_eff`; gratia cannot infer
chain boundaries from its dimensions. A supplied `chain_id` must agree with
stored metadata.

`n_draws` is the total retained count, so 2,000 draws over four chains retains
500 draws per chain. Likelihood and LOO/WAIC wrappers default to 4,000 draws;
bayesplot uses 50 for ordinary checks and 4,000 for leave-one-out plots.
Supplied matrices determine their own count and chains. These wrappers reject
the obsolete `n` argument, and inactive sampler controls produce errors.
Use `diagnostics = TRUE` directly in `log_lik()`, or in `sampling_args` for LOO
and bayesplot, to retain coefficient diagnostics. The likelihood matrix also
supports `as_mcmc_draws()` for diagnostics of its observation-wise log densities.

`log_lik()`, `loo::loo()` and `loo::waic()` cover supported GAMs, BAMs and
{scam} fits for which the responses are independent given the model coefficients.
Full `gamm()` and `gamm4()` fits, BAMs with residual correlation, quasi families,
Cox partial likelihoods and censored observation processes are outside this
likelihood support. For ordinary posterior predictive checks, the supported
model classes and conditioning options vary with the plot type.
[`diagnostic_support`](../reference/diagnostic_support.html)

With random-effect smooths, leaving out one observation at a time assesses
prediction within the fitted groups when each group has other observations.
To assess prediction for new groups, leave out entire groups.

The script `inst/validation/loo-refits.R` compares PSIS results with explicit
leave-one-out refits in Gaussian, Poisson and binomial examples. Some refits
hold the smoothing and other family parameters at their full-data estimates.
Others re-estimate them in each refit.
